# jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit

Git teaches a three-layer story: working tree, index/staging area, commits. Most day-to-day anxiety — "did I stage that?", "is this amend or a new commit?", "how do I undo the last amend?" — lives in the gaps between those layers. **Jujutsu (`jj`)** collapses the gap: the working copy *is* a real commit (`@`). Every edit is snapshotted into that commit the next time you run a `jj` command. There is no staging area to reconcile. Undo is an operation-log rewind. This chapter builds that mental model on a colocated Git repo, runs the handful of commands you need every day (`jj new`, `jj describe`, `jj squash`, `jj undo`), and shows how remotes still speak Git.

Verified against **jj 0.46.0** on x86_64 Linux (2026-10-09). Primary docs: <https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/>.

## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you can:

- Explain why `@` is a commit ID that changes as you type  
- Distinguish **change ID** (stable) from **commit ID** (content-addressed, rewritten)  
- Colocate jj on an existing Git checkout with `jj git init`  
- Start a fresh change (`jj new`), describe it, fold WIP with `jj squash`, and rewind with `jj undo`  
- Push to a Git remote without abandoning Git-speaking collaborators  

## Thesis

> In Git, a commit is what you produce when you are *done*. In jj, a commit is what you are *editing*. The working copy is not a waiting room — it is revision `@`, rewritten in place until you say `jj new`.

That single flip removes the index. Files you create are tracked automatically (subject to `.gitignore` and `snapshot.auto-track`). Files you delete are untracked automatically. `jj st` both reports and snapshots.

## Mental model

```text
Git mental layers              jj mental layers
─────────────────              ────────────────
working tree  ─┐
staging index ─┼─→ commit      working-copy commit @  ←── you edit files here
               ┘               parent commit      @-
                               operation log      (every jj command)
```

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `@` | Working-copy commit — rewritten on almost every `jj` command when files changed |
| `@-` | Parent of `@` (usually the last "finished" change) |
| Change ID | Stable identifier for a logical change (survives rewrites); prefer this in daily use |
| Commit ID | Git-compatible content hash; changes whenever the snapshot changes |
| Operation | One recorded `jj` action; `jj undo` rewinds the latest |

## Case 0 — install and version

```bash
# jj 0.46.0 — verify yours
jj --version
```

```text
jj 0.46.0-7d382314f9420b4b8d932245b49c99492c812b9f
```

Configure identity once (required before any push to a Git remote):

```bash
jj config set --user user.name "Your Name"
jj config set --user user.email "you@example.com"
```

## Case 1 — colocated repo: Git and jj share one working tree

```bash
# demo.sh — colocated init and first snapshot
rm -rf /tmp/jj-wc-demo && mkdir /tmp/jj-wc-demo && cd /tmp/jj-wc-demo
jj git init --colocate
echo 'hello' > README.md
jj status
```

```text
Initialized repo in "."
Working copy changes:
A README.md
Working copy  (@) : rukslwvq 762e295b (no description set)
Parent commit (@-): zzzzzzzz 00000000 (empty) (no description set)
```

What just happened:

1. `jj git init --colocate` created both `.jj/` and `.git/` in the same directory (the default for Git-backed workspaces).  
2. Adding `README.md` and running `jj status` **snapshotted** the file into `@`. There was no `git add`.  
3. `@` already has a change ID (`rukslwvq…`) and a commit ID (`762e295b…`). The commit ID will change on the next rewrite; the change ID will not.

On an *existing* Git clone the same command works from inside the checkout: `jj git init` (colocate is the default). jj imports Git refs and keeps exporting on every command so `git log` / `git status` stay coherent — usually with Git in a detached-HEAD-looking state, which is normal for colocated workflows.

## Case 2 — describe, then `jj new` when the change is "done enough"

```bash
jj describe -m 'add README'
jj log -r 'all()' --limit 5
jj new
jj log -r '@ | @-' 
```

```text
Working copy  (@) now at: rukslwvq c4ec738f add README
Parent commit (@-)      : zzzzzzzz 00000000 (empty) (no description set)
@  rukslwvq … c4ec738f
│  add README
◆  zzzzzzzz root() 00000000
Working copy  (@) now at: pslozopm e8dc9b58 (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : rukslwvq c4ec738f add README
```

`jj describe` rewrote `@` (new commit ID, same change ID, now with a message). `jj new` created an *empty* successor and moved `@` there. The finished work sits at `@-`. That is the jj equivalent of "commit what I staged and start fresh" — except nothing was staged.

## Case 3 — keep editing, then squash (or edit)

```bash
echo 'world' >> README.md
jj diff
jj squash -m 'extend README'
```

```text
Modified regular file README.md:
   1    1: hello
        2: world
Working copy  (@) now at: lyxlzlzu … (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : rukslwvq 66cd1710 extend README
```

`jj squash` moves the changes from `@` into its parent (default) and leaves you on a new empty working-copy commit. It is the boring "amend the previous change with my current WIP" path. The alternative is `jj edit <change>` to resume amending an older change directly in `@` — useful when the change is still open; squash-then-diff is clearer when you want a reviewable delta first.

## Case 4 — undo is not reflog archaeology

```bash
jj undo
jj log -r 'all()' --limit 8
```

```text
Undid operation: … squash commits into …
Working copy  (@) now at: pslozopm 241153d1 (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : rukslwvq c4ec738f add README
@  pslozopm … 241153d1
│  (no description set)
○  rukslwvq … c4ec738f
│  add README
◆  zzzzzzzz root() 00000000
```

Every `jj` command records an **operation**. `jj undo` rewinds the last one (here: the squash). The working-copy files and the commit graph return to the prior operation. For deeper recovery: `jj op log`, then `jj op undo` / restore by operation id. This is why "I amended the wrong thing" stops being an emergency.

## Interop with Git remotes

Colocated repos still push with Git semantics:

```bash
# Create a bookmark (jj's branch-like movable ref) on the finished change
jj bookmark create my-feature -r @-
jj git push --bookmark my-feature
# Or let jj mint a name from a change id:
# jj git push --change @-
```

Notes for Git teammates:

- They clone and work with plain Git; the `.jj/` directory is yours.  
- Prefer bookmarks for anything that must be named on the remote.  
- After `jj git push`, if `@` became immutable, jj creates a fresh working-copy commit on top — run `jj new` yourself if you need a clean empty `@` before more edits.  
- Mixing `git` mutation commands in a colocated workspace works but is easier if you mostly stay in `jj` and treat `git` as the remote transport / blame / bisect tool.

## The trap

- **Looking for `git add`.** There isn't one. Ignore files with `.gitignore`; untrack with `jj file untrack` after ignoring.  
- **Treating commit IDs as stable handles.** Use change IDs (`jj log` shows them first). Commit IDs churn every snapshot.  
- **Pushing `@` when it is empty WIP.** Push `@-` or an explicit bookmark on the finished change (`jj git push --change @-`).  
- **Expecting Git's staging partial-hunk workflow by default.** jj snapshots the whole working copy; use `jj split`, `jj squash -i`, or file-level tools when you need to carve hunks.  
- **Forgetting identity config.** Until `user.name` / `user.email` are set, commits are empty-identity and remotes will reject them.

## The boring rule

Edit freely. Let `@` absorb the snapshot. When the change is ready enough, `jj describe` + `jj new` (or `jj squash` into the parent). Wrong move? `jj undo`. Speak Git at the boundary with bookmarks and `jj git push`.

## Try this

1. `jj git init --colocate` inside a throwaway Git repo you already know.  
2. Make three file edits; run `jj st` after each; watch the commit ID of `@` change while the change ID stays put.  
3. `jj new`, edit again, `jj squash`, `jj undo`, confirm the diff returns.  
4. `jj bookmark create demo -r @- && jj git push --bookmark demo` to a personal fork.
